messages.author: 92555aa28f92a6ba
messages.subject: Model Validation and testing
parts:
Hi Simmer crew,

Do you have any recommendations on model validation? Coming from a ML background I tend to try split my data into training, validation and testing. Do you have any recommended reading around how to test models? In particular, looking at metrics that test if temporal flow if being modeled correctly. 

There also appears to be a tendency to simulate the inputs into a model, what advantage does this have over using historical data other than in extrapolation?

Thank you for the great work on simmer. 

Best,

Andre

messages.author: a5b521959296c79e
messages.subject: Re: Model Validation and testing
parts:
Verification and validation of simulation models (especially Discrete Event models) is a topic that has been studied in depth for a very long time.
There is almost always a tutorial given each year at the Winter Simulation Conference, for which proceedings are publicly available.
https://informs-sim.org/

Also, an introduction to the topic can be found in most any undergraduate discrete event simulation textbook.

messages.author: 57a7662e790ccc92
messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Re: Model Validation and testing
parts:
Validation means different things in different contexts. In ML you're holding some data back to validate the model fit to the data. When doing DES you're constructing a model programmatically, a very different exercise than fitting. It's probably a fairly complicated model (unless you assume multivariate queuing theory to be simple). So what I do is for the first step is validate any known physical constraints of the system. For example, in a patient disease simulation -- do all trajectories die at most once? This is more similar to debugging than validation at this stage, but it's a great first step. Are there any constraints on the system must be satisfied. Spot auditing trajectories at random is an excellent exercise, making sure to pull at least one containing every possible event.

The next step is seeing if the parameters of the model be tweaked in such a way that grossly simplify the model to a known one. If so, run all these identified parameter sets simulations and compare with known simple models. For example, in disease simulation I turn off secular death from competing risks, and make the odds of all complications but one incredibly small. Then running the model, does the simulation reproduce the marginal rate and known distributions? I.e. can it reproduce a known simple model with restricted parameters? The general focus here is validating each parameter (or a minimal set of parameters) has the desired influence when everything that can be turned off is.

Next, are there published similar complex models that I can set the parameters to match? For example, in our upcoming paper we have 3 conditions we investigate as competing risks. A well known model already exists for one of the conditions, and it was constructed by a very different method. So we turn off the 2 conditions not published and run the model with the parameters from the published one and see if one can reproduce the results. For our case our model fortunately reproduced the published result and the manuscript is under minor revision at present.
